Food presets Brands Chart Guide EN English Español Português Français Deutsch About air-fryer-to-convection conversion An air fryer recipe scales badly. The basket holds one layer, and the moment you are feeding six instead of two, a convection oven — the same fan-driven heat in a cavity big enough for two sheet pans — is the faster route. Because both appliances move hot air with a fan, going from an air fryer to a convection oven is a small adjustment, not the full trip back to a conventional oven. This converter adds back only the per-food gap between the two: a few degrees and a little time, using the same table as the convection-to-air-fryer converter, run backward. When a convection oven beats the basket Batch size is the main one: a convection oven cooks two or three trays at once, with the fan keeping every rack close to the same temperature, where an air fryer would need three loads back to back. Large items — a whole chicken, a sheet of cookies, a tray bake — fit an oven and not a basket. And when the air fryer is busy with a side dish, moving the main to the fan oven gets both to the table at the same time. Sheet-pan dinners, where vegetables and a protein share one tray and finish together, are easier to time in an oven too. For one portion of fries or wings, the air fryer still wins on speed and crispness. Why the temperature often doesn't change The gap between an air fryer and a convection oven is 0–15°F, and an oven dial clicks in 25°F steps. Add 10°F to a 375°F air fryer setting and the nearest step on the dial is still 375°F. So for many foods this converter gives the same temperature back and puts the whole adjustment into time. That is the honest answer: the difference between the two appliances is mostly how fast the air reaches the food, and a slightly longer cook in the bigger cavity is how the oven makes it up. Snapping to dial steps also means a recipe converted there and back lands on the number it started from. Worked example A general air fryer setting of 340°F for 27 minutes in a basket becomes 350°F for 30 minutes in a convection oven — the fan-oven recipe it most likely started as. Fries at 390°F for 18 minutes become 400°F for 20 minutes: the dial lands on the next step up, and the oven gets a couple of extra minutes because air moves more slowly across a full tray than through a basket. Settings at your air fryer's maximum If the air fryer setting sits at the unit's ceiling — 400°F on most baskets, 450°F on oven-style units — it may itself be a converted number: a hotter convection recipe held down to what the air fryer can reach, with about 8% extra time added. The converter can't tell which, so it shows a note. If you know the recipe started out hotter, use the original convection setting instead of converting back. Convection → Air Fryer converter → Air Fryer → Oven converter (conventional oven) → Oven → Air Fryer converter → Printable conversion chart → Frozen food mode (packaging instructions) → Frequently Asked Questions How do I convert air fryer time and temperature to a convection oven? Add 0–15°F depending on the food, round to the nearest 25°F dial step, and add 5–10% to the time. The converter above does all three, using the same per-food table as the convection-to-air-fryer converter so the two directions agree. Is air fryer to convection the same as air fryer to oven? No. A conventional, fan-off oven needs 20–25°F and 15–30% of the time added back. A convection oven already has a fan, so it needs much less. If your oven has no fan setting, use the Air Fryer → Oven converter instead. Why did the temperature come out the same as my air fryer setting? Because the gap between the two appliances is smaller than one 25°F step on an oven dial. Rounding to a setting your oven can actually show often lands back on the air fryer number, so the adjustment goes into the time instead. Should I use convection bake or convection roast? Convection bake suits most foods. Convection roast, which adds the top element, helps wings, potatoes, and anything you want crisp. Use the temperature the converter gives either way. Do I need extra time with two trays in the oven? Often a few minutes, yes. The converted time assumes one tray with room around it. With two or more, rotate the trays halfway and check a minute or two after the converted time. Do internal temperature targets change? No. Poultry is done at 165°F internal and fish, steak, or chops at 145°F, in an air fryer or a convection oven.
